paragraphs: In the nineteenth year of Jianyuan, on the eve of the eighth anniversary of Wang Meng’s death, a north wind rose over Chang’an.

At the third watch Empress Gou was still awake. She hung an old fur robe beside the lamp to warm it. The fur at its collar had worn thin; Fu Jian had worn it on his expedition to Hexi several years before. A palace attendant brought in a memorial prayer from the Ministry of Ceremonies. Finding the Heavenly King asleep over his desk, he was about to withdraw quietly. Empress Gou took the scroll from him and set it by the lamp without a word.
When Fu Jian awoke, the first thing he saw was the robe. He frowned. “You’ve brought this out again.”
“The wind is fierce beyond the walls.”
“A few steps to Jinglüe’s tomb won’t freeze me to death.”
Empress Gou straightened his sash. “Eight years ago you came back from the tomb and burned with fever for two days. You said it wouldn’t freeze you to death then, too.”

Fu Jian did not argue further. The candlelight caught a fine line of white at his temples. The empress reached out to smooth his loosened hair. For an instant he remembered adjusting the corner of Wang Meng’s quilt in much the same way before the man died. After middle age, old memories often returned first in small gestures.

More than three years had passed since the defeat on the Huai. Peng Chao’s case had been settled. The military roads along the river had been repaired and broken again; fresh grain had reached the Xiangyang granaries; and year by year the Jin boats north of the Yangtze had multiplied. Military rolls in several northern provinces still counted some men twice. Disputes over the old troops surrendered by members of the imperial clan had not ceased. The paper samples and missing couriers in the old Right Guard case were not yet fully accounted for. The pines along Wang Meng’s tomb road, meanwhile, had grown taller. When Fu Jian passed east of the city and glimpsed that patch of green from afar, something in him always stopped for a moment.

At dawn he took no grand imperial carriage, only several hundred riders through the eastern gate. Crown Prince Fu Hong had arrived at the tomb first. In his hands were two versions of the memorial prayer, one drafted by the Ministry of Ceremonies and the other amended.
“Which line displeased you?” Fu Jian asked, dismounting.
Fu Hong handed him the original. It said, *In obedience to my lord’s dying command, we have not dared even to turn our gaze southward.*
Fu Jian read it and laughed. “Am I forbidden even to look south?”
“The ceremony officials did not dare choose different words without leave.”
“What did you change?”
*Remembering my lord’s last counsel, we proceed with caution before sending armies south.*
“Proceed with caution—or do not send them at all?”
Fu Hong looked toward the tombstone. Only after a long silence did he say, “As of today, we do not yet know.”

Fu Jian did not much like this answer. Inside and outside the palace, many people had learned to say *I do not know* when what they sought was a word of pardon from him. But his son had laid the revised prayer beside the recent grain-convoy register from Xiangyang. This time, he understood, it was no evasion.
“You spent last night at the Secretariat again?”
“The military rolls took longer than expected.”
“Or were you afraid that, once a southern campaign was proposed, no one would remember the old accounts?”

Fu Hong did not answer. Fu Jian took the brush from him, tapped twice beside the words *with caution*, and signaled that the ceremonial officers should read that version. Father and son went up the cold, damp stone steps to the altar. The wind lifted a ritual banner and exposed the dense rows of stitches on the back of its embroidery.

Beside the altar, two old ministers were arguing over those two words. One said *with caution* suited the condition of the realm better than *dare not*; the other called it a sign that a campaign against Jin had already been decided. The argument died as Fu Jian approached. Farther off, an elderly ceremonial clerk walked slowly with a bronze tray and was urged to hurry by a younger colleague. He stumbled into a quicker step. An old bronze wine cup fell from the tray and rang down several tomb steps. The old clerk bent his trembling knees to retrieve it, but Fu Jian told him not to kneel. The sovereign went down two steps and picked it up himself.

A nick remained in the bronze cup from the first rites performed for Wang Meng. Fu Jian rubbed the hollow with his thumb and dimly recalled something Wang Meng had still been worried about on his sickbed: a grain official in Nanyang had withheld the wages of civilian carters. So many stern edicts had been issued in eight years. Who knew whether that family had ever received its pay? Fu Jian returned the cup to the tray without asking. If he asked, he knew, the men behind him would certainly produce a satisfactory answer.

When the rites ended, Fu Jian did not immediately return to the palace. He summoned his ministers to a side residence near the tomb. Some had been on their feet all morning and their knees were stiff. Hearing that they were to sit in council now, they exchanged uneasy looks. The charcoal burned hot in braziers indoors, while outside the shuttered windows pine needles rustled softly.
“Eight years,” Fu Jian said.
The Minister of Ceremonies rose to recite Wang Meng’s achievements, but Fu Jian raised a hand to stop him.
“We have just heard all that. What I ask you today is whether, for the two years remaining, we shall still keep the ten-year promise made at Jinglüe’s deathbed.”

An elder of the imperial clan spoke first. Wang Meng, he said, had feared the north was not yet settled and the old Qiang and Yan followers too difficult to control. Now most tiger tallies had been returned to the throne, and Qin armies had won victories from Hexi to Xiangyang. Circumstances had changed. Others said that a man of resolve must act according to his times and should not turn a dead chancellor’s last words into a law of Heaven. Another offered rumors of struggles for power at the Jin court, arguing that the great clans of Jiankang were at odds. If Qin waited until Xie Xuan had completed his flotilla defenses on the Huai, it would lose its chance.
The room grew quieter when Fu Pi rose. Since the victory at Xiangyang, he was no longer the young prince whose only answer had been to demand more soldiers from his father.

“I ask leave to train a river fleet,” he said. “I still remember our defeat on the Huai. If we face such floating bridges and shallows again, let the boats and grain be ready ahead of the infantry. We need not send armored men wading into the river once more.”
“How many ships? Who will build them?” Fu Rong asked.

Fu Pi recited a series of figures without hesitation. He had indeed spent years collecting procedures from Jiang-Huai boatbuilders. Fu Rong listened, then asked who would replace the western garrisons when they were transferred south, and whether the grain allocated for an expedition could be recovered if Guanzhong suffered another drought. Fu Pi’s answers became slower.
Murong Chui stood by the window. Suddenly he said, “We cannot fill the home garrisons with the old and infirm just to make up the numbers. I have seen how Yan’s lines of retreat were cut.”
The ministers turned toward him.

“If the southern expedition comes next year, the troops in Hebei need at least two more rounds of training. Otherwise the vanguard may win while men in the rear raise the old Yan banner. Whom would Your Majesty send home first to put down the rebellion?”

The word *Yan* fell heavily in that room. Having spoken, Murong Chui too went silent. He had been among the men Wang Meng distrusted most in life; now, beside Wang Meng’s tomb, he was counting the gaps in the Qin garrisons of Hebei.

Yao Chang sat in the last row. He had lost command of the Right Guard after the Wei Bridge affair but still attended the rites as Minister of Ceremonies. When Fu Jian saw him sitting silent for so long, he asked, “Minister Yao, you used to urge me toward a southern campaign more eagerly than anyone. Why so quiet today?”
“I now oversee rites, not troops. I fear that if I say too much, suspicion will follow.”
“I wish you to speak.”

Yao Chang stood, unhurried. “Two years can be long or short. Your Majesty is praised throughout the realm for honoring a promise. Yet if in those two years the Xie clan fortifies the Huai and the Jin court pulls itself together, there will be men in the future who blame you for the opportunity lost today. I fear that, in keeping faith with Lord Wang, Your Majesty may forget that the living have hopes as well.”
Fu Rong asked coldly, “Are there more men who wish to cross the Yangtze, or more who wish to bring their fathers and brothers home from the army? Have you asked them all, Minister Yao?”
Yao Chang was not angered. “The Prince of Yangping asks about grain. I ask about time. Both questions deserve to be asked.”
Fu Jian looked from one man to the other, then settled his gaze on Murong Chui. “And you?”
“If ten years were promised, let ten years pass in full.”
“Jinglüe is gone. Must he still make my decisions for me?”

“When I served Yan, I saw rulers reverse their decrees from morning to evening. Changing an order is easy. What is hard is finding anyone who will trust the next one.” Murong Chui paused. “And even if Your Majesty ordered a march today, we still lack the boats and dependable grain roads.”
Fu Pi lowered his head. He had hoped his figures for shipbuilding would prove how much he had changed, yet Murong Chui would not help persuade Fu Jian.
Fu Hong had not raised his hand in objection once. Only when Fu Jian called upon him did he slide a thin ledger forward. Its cover bore two characters: *To Be Verified*.
“What is this?”

“The numbers who can leave their camps for an expedition from Guanzhong, Luoyang, and Xiangyang. I have included only those for whom there is proof. A military office may report thirty thousand, but some of those men are actually farming garrison land. Of three thousand fit to fight, five hundred must stay on the road to guard the grain. And every man taken from home for war is one less man to bring in the harvest.”
“How many are there altogether?”
“I cannot total them yet.”
Fu Jian’s face darkened.

Fu Hong went on. “I have first struck out duplicate registrations. Men listed under two different camps are not being counted until we know where they serve. If Father wants a number, the Secretariat can supply one in a few days. If Father means to send an army on the strength of that number, we must go into the provinces and see the men.”

A piece of charcoal split in the brazier, scattering tiny sparks. Fu Jian looked at the ink marks on his son’s cuffs. The boy who once stood behind him holding edicts had scarcely dared step down from a dais without looking to his father for permission. Now, before the royal kinsmen and generals, he was saying that the emperor could not yet have the number he wanted.
“I promised Jinglüe ten years,” Fu Jian began slowly. “I did not know then how quickly ten years could pass.”
No one in the room answered.
“I shall keep my promise.”
Fu Pi raised his head. Yao Chang bowed his clasped hands and lowered his eyes. Murong Chui relaxed his fingers from his leather belt, his expression unchanged.

“But,” Fu Jian continued, “I cannot wait until the tenth year’s last day before asking how many soldiers this realm can truly put in the field. The central army must count men fit to fight. The Secretariat must count households, grain, carts, and horses. The Prince of Yangping must inspect the roads and river journeys. Remove false figures, and keep in the count the men who must remain on guard. Write down who still remembers how we were beaten on the Huai, and how it happened.”
“What deadline shall we set?” Fu Rong asked.
“One year.”
“And if the verified numbers are insufficient after a year?”
“We shall consider it again.”
“And if they are sufficient?”
Fu Jian gazed through the window at the stand of young pines. “We shall consider it again then, too.”

After the ministers departed, Fu Jian stayed by the tomb for half a day. He sent the guards farther away and kept only a flask of warm water. Of all that had happened by the sickbed eight years before, what he remembered most clearly now was Wang Meng coughing blood, then suddenly asking: how many people had died along the grain roads? At the time, Fu Jian had seldom seen the dead by the roadside himself. He had seen only the great totals forwarded by the Secretariat.

He crouched and brushed the earth from the base of the stele. “Jinglüe,” he murmured, “we took Xiangyang. Then we lost on the Huai. You told me to wait ten years. You were right that there would still be so much left undone.”
Wind moved through the branches. For a long while he said nothing more.
“But Xie An is waiting too. If one day I do cross the Yangtze, what formation do you suppose he will lay on the opposite bank?”

The tombstone did not answer. In the distance a herdsman returning late led a thin ox along the path, its neck bell sounding slowly. Fu Jian rose and suddenly felt he had asked the wrong man. Wang Meng had spent his life making plans for him, but he had long ago left the hardest matter in his hands: whether to cross the river or halt the army, the living would have to bear the decision.

As they prepared to leave, Fu Hong lagged behind and saw his father rest a hand against the tombstone. A long time passed before he let go. Fu Hong wanted to go forward and offer some comfort, but in the end said nothing. In his youth his father had gathered heroes from every quarter by sheer courage. Now the son could see that courage itself could also be a burden. Even if the registers of the Secretariat did not yet justify a southern war, many at court would rather write down a page of beautiful figures for the Heavenly King than risk being thought cowards.

On the journey back, Fu Hong’s carriage passed the common burial ground of those killed in the old Wei Bridge mutiny. The elms planted a few years earlier were already as tall as men, though faded strips of cloth still hung before the graves. The driver asked whether to stop. Fu Hong said there was no need. Too many documents awaited him that day, and stopping would give him nothing new to say to the dead. He only ordered that, during the new military audit, the names of men no longer in camp—including those buried here—be struck one by one from the old rolls, lest someone continue drawing army pay in their names.

That night a new edict to audit military affairs went out from Chang’an. It ordered no army south against Jin. It required only a verified accounting of available soldiers, boatbuilding materials, stored grain, troops needed for home defense, and transport routes in every province. Fu Rong had the required evidence specified item by item. Household totals were not to be passed off as soldiers, nor grain still sitting in a granary counted as rations already available to the front. The Secretariat also sent Zhu Xu a letter asking him to describe the roads and ordinary boats of the Jiang-Huai region during the rains, without asking about Jin fortifications. Zhu Xu received it, placed it beside his lamp, and did not put brush to paper.

The carriage workshops of Luoyang heard the news and raised timber prices even before the southeastern provinces did. A horse breeder in Hedong, hearing that the court meant to inspect warhorses, hurried to sell his lame animals to neighbors. A granary clerk in Xiangyang feared that old accounts would be reopened and sat up all night recounting rice sacks. Officers in Hebei, thinking a great war in the south would leave even fewer good soldiers to hold their home ground, quietly petitioned for new reviews of their units' rotation dates.

Fu Hong sat at the Secretariat receiving the first replies. Not one character in the documents spoke of “conquering Jin,” yet every line looked as though someone were calculating the stages of a long journey. Late that night he turned the final page and touched the ending of the edict written in his father’s own hand. The ink there was heavy enough to have seeped through to the back.
The crown prince remembered the three words of assent spoken beside Wang Meng’s sickbed eight years ago.
The ten years were not yet over.

Couriers were already riding one after another through the eastern gate. Their hoofbeats dwindled into the distance. Snow had not yet fallen, but the imperial road rang dry and hard in the north wind.
